topic: Why does Greenland look so large on some maps?
audience: Adult used to flat world maps
prior: May assume every map has one fixed scale and area can be compared by eye.
objective: Distinguish a real area difference from Mercator scale distortion.
takeaway: Mercator enlarges area increasingly toward the poles.

sources.G2: Natural Earth public-domain outline snapshot, episodes/coastlines.json

editorial_direction: Open on Greenland and South America in the same Mercator view.
misconceptions: All flat maps stretch area in the same way

chapters.question: Which shape looks bigger on that map?
chapter_claims: Name spherical Mercator. Compare the same Greenland and mainland South America outlines.
stages: Trace the same geographic vertices on a globe.

mercator: Mercator exaggerates Greenland's size relative to South America. The two land masses do not have the same real area; South America is larger.
globe: This is a globe view of the same underlying geographic outlines. South America covers a larger area on Earth. The view from one angle is not itself an area measurement.

chapters.question: What does flattening do at high latitude?
chapter_claims: Mercator longitude lines are parallel. Scale increases with absolute latitude.
stages: Keep identities across a view change.

globe: Meridians meet at the poles on the globe. Greenland is at high northern latitude; South America straddles the equator.
mercator: Mercator plots meridians as parallel vertical lines and enlarges the scale farther from the equator. It preserves local angles, not areas.

chapters.question: Can we isolate the scale change?
chapter_claims: Two patches have equal area on the sphere; the patch at 60 degrees is larger in Mercator than that at the equator.
stages: Show both equal-on-Earth patches in Mercator.

mercator: In the Mercator map Greenland looks disproportionately large. Ask how to separate latitude distortion from different land sizes.
patches: The two highlighted patches, one near sixty degrees north and one on the equator, have equal area on Earth. The northern patch looks larger on Mercator. The comparison is about patches, not equal-size continents.

chapters.question: What if the comparison is specifically about area?
chapter_claims: A cylindrical equal-area check preserves area ratios, not shape; no numerical area ratio is given.

mercator: Recall Mercator's distortion toward the poles. Two places need not look proportional to their underlying areas.
equal-area: The equal-area projection preserves relative area. Greenland and South America remain different sizes, with South America larger. Shapes can still look distorted.

transfer.question: How can we check a real size difference?
transfer.answer: Use an equal-area projection or geodesic areas.
